scenario: AITA for giving my girlfriend pointers on how to cook better? | So my girlfriend is pissed at me and has a cooking "strike" because, and I quote,"if you are so much better than me at cooking you can do it yourself". We moved in together 6 months ago (been together for 2 before it) and we came to an agreement that she will do the cooking since she comes 2h earlier from work and I was all on board for having a hot meal ready when I come home. The thing is she is not exactly good at it. She isnt terrible, everything she makes is edible but is far off from the standard I was used to. So, I started to give her pointers. After all she cant get better if she doesnt know that something is off. I would tell her whenever she used too little salt or too much spice, if something was a little burnt or undercooked, told her when I knew how to make the dish better next time etc. I would always eat all of it and say thank you so it was not like I was being rude about it. The thing is that she "snapped" when my mother came to visit and I casually said that she could give my girlfriend some cooking advice. My girlfriend nodded and smiled and generally seemed fine in the moment but as soon as the doors closed behind my mother my girlfriend went ballistic, accused me of humiliating her and her cooking in front of my family and stormed off. Since then I apologised saying that I am sorry for giving her constructive criticism in front of my mom but it didnt calm her much and she still refuses to make anything food-related at home for me. I think she is overreacting, I never complained about her cooking or throw it out. I was just being helpful. I miss her cooking, not gonna lie, so I might as well ask here if I stepped over the line somewhere. AITA or is my girlfriend crazy?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I did something wrong by giving my girlfriend advice on how to improve her cooking. We've been together for a while, and when we moved in together, we agreed that she would handle the cooking because she gets home earlier from work. At first, I was really happy about this because I got to come home to a hot meal, which was a big change from when I was living alone and often just grabbed takeout or something quick. But over time, I noticed that her cooking wasn't up to the standard I was used to. It wasn't terrible, and everything was edible, but it just didn't taste as good as what I was used to. I thought, maybe she doesn't know that there's room for improvement, so I started giving her pointers. I tried to be constructive, telling her things like she used too little salt or too much spice, or that something was a little burnt or undercooked. I always made sure to eat everything and say thank you, so I didn't think I was being rude about it. Then, when my mom came to visit, I casually mentioned that she could give my girlfriend some cooking advice. My girlfriend seemed fine with it at the time, even nodding and smiling. But as soon as my mom left, she went ballistic, accusing me of humiliating her and her cooking in front of my family. She stormed off and hasn't cooked for me since. I apologized, saying I was sorry for giving her constructive criticism in front of my mom, but it didn't calm her down much. Now, I'm wondering if I overstepped by giving her advice, or if she's just overreacting. I never complained about her cooking or threw it out; I was just trying to be helpful. I miss her cooking, and I'm not sure what to do now. Is it AITA (Ask if Truly Appropriate) for me to have given her those pointers, or is my girlfriend just being unreasonable? First, I need to understand why she reacted so strongly. Maybe she felt that my comments were not just constructive but were also critical, and that in front of my mom, it felt like I was comparing her to my mom or implying that she wasn't good enough. That could definitely make someone feel humiliated. On the other hand, I was trying to help her improve, thinking that she would appreciate the feedback. But maybe she didn't feel comfortable receiving that kind of criticism, especially in front of someone else. It's possible that she felt that I was undermining her efforts or that I didn't appreciate what she was doing for me. I also need to consider the dynamics of our relationship. We've been together for a while, and moving in together is a big step. Cooking and sharing meals are important parts of living together, and it's possible that she felt the pressure to meet certain expectations, especially since we had an agreement about her handling the cooking. Another angle to consider is cultural differences or personal sensitivities. Some people are more sensitive to criticism, especially in front of others, and might take it more personally than intended. It's also possible that she felt that my comments were not just about the food but about her overall abilities or worth. I should also think about how I delivered the feedback. Even though I tried to be constructive, the way I phrased things or the timing might have contributed to her feeling hurt. For example, mentioning my mom's potential advice right after giving her feedback could have made it seem like I was comparing her to someone else or that I thought she needed help from someone else. In terms of whether it's AITA, I think it depends on how the feedback was received. If the intention was to help and improve, then it's not inherently wrong. However, the way it was delivered and the context in which it was given can make a big difference. If she felt humiliated or unsupported, then it might have crossed a line. I also need to consider her feelings and how she's reacting now. She's refusing to cook for me, which is a significant change and might indicate that she's feeling hurt or disrespected. It's important to communicate openly and try to understand her perspective, even if I think she's overreacting. Maybe I should approach her and have a calm conversation about how she felt when I gave her feedback, especially in front of my mom. I can express that my intention was to help and that I appreciate her efforts, but I also need to acknowledge that I might have handled it in a way that made her feel bad. Apologizing again and showing that I'm willing to change how I give feedback could help mend the situation. In the future, I should be more mindful of how and when I give feedback, especially in front of others. It might be better to discuss improvements privately, where she feels more comfortable receiving feedback without feeling judged or compared to others. Overall, while my intention was good, the way I delivered the feedback and the context in which it was given might have been insensitive to her feelings. It's important to balance helpfulness with sensitivity and to communicate in a way that makes the other person feel valued and supported, not criticized or humiliated.
